messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared, Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Moshe is a 63-year-old rabbi who has led a small congregation in a Midwestern suburb for nearly two decades, but the man who stands at the bimah each Shabbat is not the same man who arrived in America thirty years ago. The event that reshaped his life happened in the winter of 1993, when he was still living in a city that had once felt like home. Armed men had come to his neighborhood in the middle of the night, shouting orders in a language that turned every familiar street into a trap. Moshe had been hiding in a crawlspace beneath a neighbor’s floorboards, his wife’s hand clamped over her own mouth, when a booted foot landed inches from his face and a rifle butt slammed through the planks above him. The shouting had been what broke something inside him—not the gunfire, not the splintering wood, but the sound of men’s voices raised in violent command, the certainty that they could find him if they wanted to. He had stayed pressed to the cold earth for eleven hours, telling himself that if he made a sound, they would kill everyone. What he remembers most now is the feeling of his own body betraying him—his heart hammering so hard he was certain the men could hear it, his hands trembling against the dirt, his stomach clenching as if his own guts were trying to escape. He had not stopped the event from happening. Somebody else would have. Somebody braver, somebody faster, somebody who had not frozen like a child while armed men tore through his home.

In the years since, Moshe has built a life that looks stable from the outside. He has a partner who loves him, a congregation that respects him, a study lined with books that have always been his refuge. But the body remembers what the mind tries to bury. When a congregant touches his shoulder unexpectedly after a service—a gesture of warmth, of gratitude—Moshe’s entire frame goes rigid. His breath catches. His skin crawls as if the hand is a blade. He has learned to smile and nod and step away, but the feeling lingers for hours, a low thrum of alarm that tells him he is not safe. He has also learned to scan every room before he enters it. He chooses his seat in the sanctuary based on how protected he feels—back to the wall, exit visible, no one sitting behind him. His partner has noticed that he will not sit in the middle of a row at restaurants or in movie theaters. He will not sit with his back to a door. There are only a handful of places where the vigilance quiets: his study, his bedroom, the small garden behind the synagogue. Everywhere else, the threat monitor runs in the background, draining his ability to concentrate on sermons, on conversations, on the simple pleasure of a meal.

The strategies Moshe has developed to manage his distress have become their own kind of prison. He distracts himself constantly—podcasts during his commute, audiobooks while he gardens, the television on low in the study even when he is trying to read. Silence is unbearable because silence is what he heard in that crawlspace, and silence is where the shouting comes back. But distraction only works for so long. When he finds himself alone with his thoughts, the self-blame rushes in. He tells himself he deserves to suffer because of what happened. He should have done something. He should have fought. He should have protected the others. A better man would have. A rabbi, of all people, should have been a source of strength, and instead he was a trembling body in the dark. These thoughts have hollowed out his capacity for intimacy. He has pulled away from his partner over the years, not through anger but through a quiet, persistent distance. Emotional closeness feels dangerous—it requires vulnerability, and vulnerability is what nearly got him killed. He does not say this aloud. He does not know how. He simply stops sharing what he feels, stops asking for comfort, stops letting anyone see the parts of himself he has come to despise.

What finally brought Moshe to seek help was a moment of failure that he could not explain away. During a memorial service for a survivor of another conflict, a member of the congregation raised his voice in grief—not shouting, not angrily, but loud enough, sharp enough—and Moshe felt his mind go blank. He lost the thread of his sermon. He stood at the lectern with his hands shaking, unable to form a sentence, while fifty faces looked up at him with trust he no longer believed he deserved. That night, he told his partner he needed to talk to someone. He is terrified that therapy will force him to go back into that crawlspace. He is equally terrified that if he does not, the space inside him will keep shrinking until there is nothing left but the memory of a boot and a shout and a man who could not save anyone.
